n: After a three-day march home from Aphek, David's men find that Amalekite raiders have struck the south, attacked Ziklag, and burned it while the men were away.

f.g: Hebrew Negev, the dry southern region.

n: The raiders captured the women and everyone else but killed no one — likely planning to sell them as slaves. There is still hope.
David and his men arrive to find the city burned and their wives and children taken captive.
The hardened warriors weep until they have no strength left to weep. Even strong people need to grieve.
David's own two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, are among the captives. His loss is as personal as everyone else's.
In their grief, David's men talk of stoning him. At his lowest point, David “encouraged himself in the LORD his God” — he found strength in God when everything else failed.

f.w: David encouraged himself in the LORD his God
the soul of all the people was grieved

n: David asks Abiathar the priest to bring the ephod so he can seek the Lord's direction — the first time in a while that David is shown inquiring of God.
David asks whether to pursue the raiders and whether he will catch them. The Lord promises he will overtake them and recover everything.
David and his six hundred men set out and reach the Besor ravine, a streambed in the Negev.

f.g: A seasonal stream (wadi) south of Ziklag.

n: Two hundred men are too exhausted to cross the ravine, so David continues with four hundred. They had already marched three days before this.
In a field they find an Egyptian, near death, and bring him to David. They give him bread and water — kindness that will be rewarded.
They give him fig cake and raisins, and he revives; he had gone three days without food or water.

f.w: his spirit came again to him

n: The Egyptian explains he was a slave of an Amalekite who abandoned him when he fell sick three days ago. A man cast aside becomes the key to victory.
He confirms that his group raided the Negev regions of the Cherethites, Judah, and Caleb, and burned Ziklag.

f.g: A people related to the Philistines, possibly from Crete; some later served as David's bodyguard.

n: David asks him to lead them to the raiders. He agrees if David swears not to kill him or return him to his master.
He leads them to the Amalekites, who are spread out across the land celebrating — eating, drinking, and dancing over their huge plunder. They are completely off guard.
David attacks from dusk until the evening of the next day. Only four hundred young men escape on camels.

f.g: Could be either dusk or dawn.

n: David recovers everything the Amalekites took, including his two wives — just as the Lord promised.
Nothing is missing — not the young or old, sons or daughters, or plunder. David recovered all. God's promise is fulfilled to the last detail.
David also takes the Amalekites' own flocks and herds, which the men drive ahead, calling them “David's spoil.”
David returns to the two hundred men left at the Besor ravine. They come out to meet him, and he greets them warmly.
Some selfish, worthless men among David's fighters say the two hundred should get only their families back, not any plunder.
David refuses. The victory and the plunder came from the Lord, who protected them and gave them victory. It is not theirs to hoard.

f.w: that which the LORD hath given us

n: David sets a principle: those who guard the supplies share equally with those who fight. Everyone's role matters.

f.w: as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff

n: David makes this a permanent rule in Israel from that day on — a mark of his fair and generous leadership.
Back at Ziklag, David sends gifts from the plunder to the elders of Judah, calling it plunder from the Lord's enemies. This generosity builds goodwill with the people who will soon make him king.
The gifts go to towns throughout southern Judah. This Bethel is likely a southern town (Bethul), not the famous Bethel in the north.

f.g: Probably Bethul or Bethuel in the Negev.

n: More towns receive gifts — Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa — places that had supported David during his fugitive years.
Gifts also go to Rachal and to the towns of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites, clans associated with Judah.
Hormah, Chor-ashan, and Athach also receive a share.
Finally Hebron and every place David and his men had roamed receive gifts. Hebron is significant: there David will soon be anointed king of Judah.

f.g: used to frequent, used to roam
